core: what a partnership is: a business owned by two or more people who agree to operate it together for profit (working definition, attributed to OpenStax)
how it works: partners contribute money, property, labor, or skill; share decisions; split profits and losses per agreement (mechanics, stated simply)
the trade-off: more capital and complementary skills than a sole proprietorship, balanced against shared liability (original example)
general versus limited partners: general partners manage and carry unlimited liability; limited partners invest without day-to-day control
taxes: pass-through as the common pattern — the partnership itself does not pay income tax; partners report shares on personal returns (jurisdiction caveat)
the partnership agreement: the document that records name, purpose, contributions, duties, profit split, and exit provisions
honest framing: partnerships run on trust; the agreement matters most when things go wrong
supporting: partnerships can be formed orally or in writing, with a written agreement recommended
partnerships are a common choice for professional-service firms and multi-owner businesses
profit sharing can be complex when contributions differ
exiting or dissolving a partnership is harder than forming one

claims.claim: A partnership is an association of two or more individuals who agree to operate a business together for profit.
Partners agree, orally or in writing, to share in the profits and losses of the joint enterprise, and each partner typically contributes money, property, labor, or skill.
Compared with a sole proprietorship, a partnership can pool more capital and more diverse skills, because two or more people contribute financial resources and complementary expertise.
In a general partnership, all partners share in management and profits, co-own the assets, each can act on behalf of the firm, and each has unlimited liability for the business's obligations.

In a limited partnership, general partners manage the business and carry unlimited liability, while limited partners have liability capped at their investment and agree not to take part in day-to-day management.

In the common pass-through pattern of partnership taxation, the partnership itself does not pay income tax on its profits; it reports how profits were divided, and each partner reports their share on their personal tax return.

A written partnership agreement is recommended to prevent later conflicts; it typically records the partnership's name and purpose, each partner's contributions, responsibilities and duties, the profit-sharing arrangement, and provisions for adding partners, resolving conflicts, and dissolving the business.
Partnerships are often compared to marriages: they run on trust between partners, and the agreement matters most when partners disagree, leave, or the business must be dissolved.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a partnership needs a written agreement: partnerships can be formed orally or in writing, but all consulted sources recommend a written partnership agreement to prevent later conflicts.
positions: OpenStax: parties agree either orally or in writing; a written agreement is recommended
Lesson treatment: written agreement presented as best practice, not a universal legal requirement

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tax treatment is jurisdiction-specific: the IRS describes the U.S. pass-through rules in detail, while OpenStax frames 'no special taxes' as a general advantage of the form.
positions: IRS (U.S.): partnership files an information return and does not pay income tax; partners report shares on personal returns
OpenStax: no special taxes as a general advantage
Lesson treatment: pass-through stated as the common pattern, with an explicit jurisdiction caveat

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many general partners a limited partnership may have: SBA says 'only one general partner,' while OpenStax says 'one or more general partners.'
positions: SBA: limited partnerships have only one general partner with unlimited liability
OpenStax: one or more general partners
Lesson treatment: kept to the general concept — limited partners invest without day-to-day control — and avoided the specific count
